3. The learned District Judge held that the testator was legally competent and mentally and physically fit and the will was executed bonafide by him and it was duly attested and registered. He however, found that as the testator was a rent-receiver the will was hit by Section 9 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 5. The only question that calls for our determination is whether the will in question is hit by Section 9 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which was in operation when the will was executed on 23-5-56, but stood repealed on 29th Poush 1372 B.S. corresponding to 14-1-66 when the testator died. 

 6. When the will was executed Section 9 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act stood as follows: 

 "9(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, on and from the date of publication of a notification under sub-section (1) of section 3, no rent-receiver specified in such notification shall, except with the previous permission of a prescribed authority, transfer his rights and interests in any estate, taluk, tenure, holding or tenancy, to which such notification relates, by private sale, gift, will, mortgage, lease, or any contract or agreement, or transfer any land in his khas possession by any such means: 

 7. Section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (Amendment) Ordinance No. XXVII of 1961 amended the above provisions and made certain additions thereto. Section 9 after amendment read as follows:- 

 "9(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, on and from the date of publication of a notification under sub-section (1) of section 3, no rent-receiver specified in such notification shall, except as provided in sub-section (1a), transfer his rights and interest, in any estate, taluk, tenure, holding or tenancy to which such notification relates, by private sale, gift, will, mortgage, lease or any contract or agreement, or transfer any land in his khas possession by any such means without the previous permission of a prescribed authority." 

 (3) Nothing contained in the foregoing sub-section shall render void any transfer which, prior to the coming into force of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Fourth Amendment) Ordinance, 1961, was not in contravention of any law for the time being in force and was legal and valid. 

 Subsequently by the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Act, (Act No VI of 1964) Sections 9 to 9D were omitted: 

 "Section 9. as already pointed out, does not place any complete embargo on transfers of khas lands but merely restricts the mode of transfer, far, all that is necessary under this section is that the prior permission of the prescribed authority should he obtained for certain kinds of transfer. The intention of this section which was in the nature of an ad-interim provision, was clearly to prevent further complications before the preparation of the record of rights or the compensation assessment roll was undertaken. But even so, this section at no stage prevented the transfer by sale or mortgage of either agricultural or non-agricultural khas lands of the class retainable under sub-section (2) of section 20 of the Act if the land so transferred did not exceed ten standard bighas. This intention has now been made abundantly clear by the total repeal of the provisions section 9 to 9D by the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Act (Act No. VI of 1964) after the record of rights and compensation assessment rolls had been prepared."
